newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani stocks may plunge if Bhutto restored.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani stocks may plunge if Bhutto restored.

text.p: Pakistani stocks may be in for a choppy ride ahead of a Supreme Court decision expected this week on whether to restore the ousted government of Benazir Bhutto, analysts said on Sunday.
They said the Karachi 100-share index could take a dive if the court reinstated Bhutto, fired by President Farooq Leghari on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
"We expect a lot of speculative activity before the court decision, which is not very clear and may go either way," senior analyst Mudassar Malik of BMA Capital Management said.
The court has indicated it will decide on Bhutto's petition against her government's dismissal before national and provincial elections set for February 3.

Malik said most investors held long positions, which they might liquidate as tension mounts over the outcome of the case. Most analysts said the market would plunge if the court ruled in Bhutto's favour.
They said a recent rise in the index was fuelled by increasing hopes that Pakistan Muslim League leader Nawaz Sharif, seen as pro-business, will win the polls.
The index rose 25.04 points, or 1.68 percent, to 1475.79 points on Sunday.
"Benazir is perceived by the market as the problem," Munir Ladha, analyst at AKD Securities said.
"She had lost credibility with international lending agencies and had she remained in power for another month our economic situation would have been worse."
Ladha said a 200-point plunge could be expected within a few days if the Bhutto government was restored.

"Bhutto no longer instills confidence or evokes new hope," he said, adding that uncertainty about the court decision had helped to check the recent rally that could have taken the index well above the 1,500-point barrier.
"The momentum is there and if Benazir is not restored, the index will touch the 1,600-point level by next week," he said.
Malik said restoration of Bhutto might not have a severely negative impact on the general economy as her government had launched structural reforms before her dismissal.
"But Benazir would have to demonstrate that she is serious in pursuing the reforms, while Sharif already has the confidence of the market," he said.
Rizwan Butt, senior analyst at KASB & Co, said the market yearned for political stability. If polls were delayed or cancelled, further confusion and uncertainty would ensue.
"Restoration of the government would mean putting the process of political consolidation into a new cumbersome and confusing situation," Butt said.
It would be hard for a Bhutto-led government to work effectively against a hostile opposition and a once-loyal president she now sees as her worst adversary, Butt said.
"Stocks is a game of hope and despair. A new set-up always inspires the market with new hopes, while dragging on with an already tested set-up may turn the market bearish," he said.
